modules.title: Population Dynamics
modules.html:
Measures of Population

Population density is the average number of persons per unit area:

$$\text{Density} = \frac{\text{Total population}}{\text{Land area}}\;\left(\text{persons per km}^2\right)$$

Vital rates are usually expressed per 1,000 persons:

$$\text{Birth rate} = \frac{\text{Live births}}{\text{Total population}}\times1000, \qquad \text{Death rate} = \frac{\text{Deaths}}{\text{Total population}}\times1000$$ $$\text{Natural increase (\%)} = \frac{\text{Birth rate}-\text{Death rate}}{10}$$

Factors Affecting Distribution

  • Physical: relief, climate, soil fertility, water supply, vegetation, mineral deposits and disease (tsetse, onchocerciasis).
  • Human: industrial development, transport, government policy, historical settlement, security and social amenities.

Densely populated areas of Nigeria include the Lagos-Ibadan axis, the Kano close-settled zone, and the Anambra-Imo-Abia belt, while low densities occur in the middle Niger-Benue trough, the Chad basin margins and the Obudu highlands.

Population Structure

The age-sex pyramid of a developing country such as Nigeria has a broad base (high proportion under 15), a narrow apex (few over 65) and a high dependency ratio:

$$\text{Dependency ratio} = \frac{\text{Population aged }0\text{-}14 + \text{aged }65+}{\text{Population aged }15\text{-}64}\times100$$

Census and Migration

A census is the official enumeration of a country's population at a given time. Uses include planning of schools, hospitals and roads, revenue allocation, delimitation of constituencies and manpower planning. Problems in Nigeria include illiteracy, poor transport in rural areas, religious and cultural objections, political manipulation, inadequate funding and mobile populations.

Migration may be internal (rural-urban, urban-rural, rural-rural) or international (emigration, immigration), permanent, seasonal or daily (commuting). Push factors include unemployment, poor amenities, insecurity, drought and land shortage; pull factors include jobs, education, medical care and social attractions. Effects are labour shortage and abandoned farms in source areas, and congestion, slums, unemployment and pressure on services in destination areas, offset by remittances and skill transfer.

examples.q: A state with an area of 25,000 sq km has a population of 5,500,000. Calculate its population density.
In a town of 400,000 people there were 14,000 births and 6,000 deaths in one year. Find the birth rate, death rate and rate of natural increase.
examples.a: Birth rate \(= \dfrac{14{,}000}{400{,}000}\times1000 = 35\) per 1,000. Death rate \(= \dfrac{6{,}000}{400{,}000}\times1000 = 15\) per 1,000. Natural increase \(= 35-15 = 20\) per 1,000, i.e. 2.0% per annum.

modules.title: Settlement Patterns and Urbanisation
modules.html:
Types and Patterns

Settlement is any place where people live and carry out their activities. Rural settlements may be nucleated (clustered), dispersed (scattered), linear or radial. Nucleation is encouraged by limited water points, defence and communal farming; dispersion by even water supply, individual land holdings and peaceful conditions.

Site and Situation

Site is the actual ground a settlement occupies (wet point, dry point, defensive, bridge point, gap town, nodal), while situation is its position in relation to the surrounding region. Examples: Lokoja is a confluence town, Kano a route centre on old trans-Saharan trade routes, and Lagos a port and bridge-point settlement.

Urban Functions and the Urban Hierarchy

Towns perform administrative, commercial, industrial, educational, religious, mining, port and tourist functions; most are multifunctional. In a hierarchy, hamlets and villages provide low-order goods and services with small spheres of influence, while cities and metropolises provide high-order services to a large hinterland.

Urbanisation

Urbanisation is the increase in the proportion of a population living in towns. It is driven by rural-urban migration, natural increase, industrialisation and administrative decisions such as the creation of new states.

  • Advantages: employment, better education and health services, markets, exchange of ideas and modernisation.
  • Problems: slums and squatter settlements, traffic congestion, unemployment and underemployment, high crime rate, pollution, water and power shortage, and pressure on housing.
  • Solutions: mass housing schemes, urban renewal, mass transit, decentralisation of industries, rural development to slow migration, and enforcement of physical planning laws.

Rural-Urban Interaction

The town supplies the countryside with manufactured goods, credit, health care and higher education, while the countryside supplies food, raw materials and labour. Improved transport and telecommunications strengthen this two-way flow.

examples.q: Give three reasons for the nucleated settlement pattern common in the Sudan savanna of Nigeria.
examples.a: (i) Water is scarce and confined to a few wells, boreholes or rivers, so houses cluster around these points; (ii) the need for defence in the past against raids led people to live together, often within walls; (iii) communal social and religious life, shared markets and cooperative farming encourage clustering, while the flat land and communal land tenure allow compact building.

examples.q: State four problems arising from rapid urbanisation in Lagos.
examples.a: (i) Acute housing shortage leading to slums such as Ajegunle and Makoko; (ii) severe traffic congestion and long commuting times; (iii) high rates of unemployment, underemployment and crime; (iv) inadequate water supply, waste disposal and drainage, causing pollution and frequent flooding.

modules.title: World Economic Activities
modules.html:
Classification

  1. Primary: extraction of natural products - farming, fishing, forestry, mining.
  2. Secondary: processing and manufacturing - textiles, cement, food processing, steel.
  3. Tertiary: services - transport, trade, banking, education, tourism.
  4. Quaternary: research, information and communication technology.

Types of Agriculture

Subsistence systems include shifting cultivation, bush fallowing and nomadic herding; commercial systems include plantation agriculture (rubber, cocoa, oil palm), extensive mechanised grain farming (Prairies, Steppes), livestock ranching (Argentina, Australia) and market gardening near cities.

Manufacturing and Industrial Location

Factors affecting the location of industry are raw materials, power supply, labour, market, transport, water, capital, land and government policy. Industries may be raw-material oriented (cement, sawmilling), market oriented (bakery, brewing, furniture) or footloose (electronics).

Transport and Trade

ModeAdvantagesLimitations
RoadFlexible, door to door, cheap over short distancesCongestion, accidents, poor maintenance
RailCarries bulky goods cheaply over long distancesFixed routes, high capital cost, slow in Nigeria
WaterCheapest for bulky international cargoSlow; needs ports and dredging
AirFastest; good for perishables and passengersVery costly; small capacity; weather dependent
PipelineContinuous flow of oil and gasOnly liquids/gases; vandalism

Trade may be internal or international; a country's balance of trade is the difference between the value of visible exports and imports. Nigeria's exports are dominated by crude oil, giving a mono-product economy that is vulnerable to price fluctuation, which is why diversification into agriculture, solid minerals and services is emphasised.

examples.q: Why are cement factories usually located near limestone deposits?
examples.a: Cement manufacture is a weight-losing process: several tonnes of limestone, clay and gypsum are needed to make one tonne of cement, so transporting the bulky raw material is far more expensive than transporting the finished product. Locating the plant at the quarry, as at Ewekoro, Sokoto, Nkalagu and Obajana, minimises transport cost and guarantees a steady supply of raw material.

examples.q: A country exported goods worth 8.4 trillion naira and imported goods worth 6.1 trillion naira in a year. Comment on its balance of trade.
examples.a: Balance of trade \(= 8.4 - 6.1 = 2.3\) trillion naira. Since exports exceed imports, the country has a favourable (surplus) balance of trade, which strengthens its foreign reserves and currency.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a use of population census data?
quiz.solution: Rainfall forecasting depends on meteorological, not census, data.

quiz.q: The movement of people from villages to towns is called
quiz.solution: It is the dominant form of internal migration in Nigeria.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a high-order service?
quiz.solution: High-order services are few, costly and serve a large sphere of influence.

quiz.q: Fishing, mining and lumbering are examples of
quiz.solution: They involve direct extraction of natural resources.

quiz.q: Which industry is best described as market oriented?
quiz.solution: Bread is bulky, perishable and gains weight, so bakeries locate near consumers.
